## What changed

**Nothing was changed on this task, because the optimizer never saw it.** The N=30 pilot's `val` split contained 2 tasks (`traces_parsec-aap2-0047` and `-0048`); this is one of the other 28. It has exactly one measurement in the whole experiment: a single trial in the reference sweep.

## What worked

The answer. **All 2 of 2** `answer_contains` assertions passed (`assertions: 1.000`) — whatever the agent did, it said the right things.

## What didn't

The trajectory. `trajectory: 0.000` against **36 demanded calls**. Because the weighting is a flat 50/50, a perfect answer with no trajectory credit scores exactly **0.500** — indistinguishable from a perfect trajectory with a worthless answer. Both appear in v1, and both read as 0.500.

This task's contract demands **36 tool calls** in a `subset` match, including `db_describe_table`, `lookup_catalog_item` and `query_provisions_db` — none of which any simulator running on 2026-08-12 exposed. One uncallable op fails the whole ordered containment, so **trajectory 1.0 was unreachable here by construction**, and half of this task's reward was never in play. Across v1 trajectory scored 1.0 on 5/5 tasks whose demanded sequence was fully callable and 0/25 of those that were not.

## What we can (or can't) learn

**That this 0.500 is the maximum this task could score, and that the 0.5 ceiling hides which half failed.** The trajectory term was not merely hard here, it was unearnable: a demanded op could not be called. So the agent scored everything that was available to it and the row still reads as half marks. A reader of the reward alone also cannot tell this task apart from `traces_parsec-aap2-0113`, which is its exact mirror image (trajectory 1.000, assertions 0.000) and is a genuinely different situation. The distinction only survives because the components and the tool-gap flag are carried per task in `results.json` — the aggregate destroys both.
